fields.Front: What is a set, in the mathematical sense?
fields.Back: An unordered collection of distinct elements, with no duplicates (e.g. {1, 2, 3}).

fields.Front: For the implication p → q, under what condition is it false?
fields.Back: Only when p is true and q is false. In every other case (p false, regardless of q) the implication is true ("vacuously true").

fields.Front: What is the contrapositive of "p → q", and is it logically equivalent to the original?
fields.Back: The contrapositive is "¬q → ¬p". Yes — it is always logically equivalent to the original implication, which is why proofs often prove the contrapositive instead.

fields.Front: What are the converse and inverse of "p → q", and are they equivalent to it?
fields.Back: Converse: "q → p". Inverse: "¬p → ¬q". Neither is logically equivalent to the original implication (though they are equivalent to each other).

fields.Front: What is the formula for the number of permutations of r items chosen from n distinct items (order matters)?
What is the formula for the number of combinations of r items chosen from n distinct items (order doesn't matter)?
What is the key question that distinguishes when to use permutations vs. combinations?
fields.Back: Does order matter? If arranging "ABC" differently from "BAC" counts as a different outcome, use permutations; if not (they're the same selection), use combinations.

fields.Front: What is the degree of a vertex in a graph?
fields.Back: The number of edges incident to that vertex (for a directed graph, split into in-degree and out-degree).

fields.Front: What is the difference between a directed graph and an undirected graph?
fields.Back: In a directed graph, each edge has a direction (an ordered pair, A → B does not imply B → A). In an undirected graph, edges are bidirectional/unordered (A—B implies B—A).

fields.Front: What does "a mod n" (a modulo n) compute?
fields.Back: The remainder when integer a is divided by n; the result always lies in the range [0, n − 1].

fields.Front: What is the difference between a relation and a function, both from set A to set B?
fields.Back: A relation is any subset of A × B (any pairing at all). A function is a relation where every element of A maps to exactly one element of B.
Union = elements in A or B (or both). Intersection = elements in both A and B.

fields.Text: A proof by induction has two parts: the {{c1::base case}} (prove the statement holds for the smallest value, e.g. n = 0 or 1) and the {{c2::inductive step}} (assume it holds for n = k, then prove it holds for n = k + 1).

In increasing order of growth rate, common Big-O classes are: {{c1::O(1)}} constant, {{c2::O(log n)}} logarithmic, {{c3::O(n)}} linear, {{c4::O(n log n)}} linearithmic, {{c5::O(n²)}} quadratic, {{c6::O(2&sup n;)}} exponential.
fields.Extra: Note: the exponential term renders as O(2^n).
